utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. There were a few preliminary matters -- yes, Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. It was announced that the Prosecution had some preliminary matters to be raised. And before I give you an opportunity to do that, Ms. Hasan, I'd like to inform the parties about the fate of the marked map yesterday. The map was marked by the witness, it has been scanned, but the marking with the red pen did not result in a legible scanned version of it, and therefore the parties are invited, together with Mr. Registrar, to use one of the breaks in which the witness would again mark exactly on that same map but now in black, make exactly the same markings over the red markings so that it then can be scanned and that we have an electronic copy that could be admitted into evidence. That was my announcement. So at least one break is already lost. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. The first matter is in relation to an exhibit that was shown yesterday, P02100. The Prosecution has received a revised translation of that. You may recall that's the one where the English says "to the Main Staff" when it should say "to the Drina Corps." The revised translation has been uploaded in e-court under document ID 0426-9441-A-ET, and we'd request that we have permission -- or the Court Officer can replace the revision with the existing translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Court Officer is instructed to replace the present translation by the newly uploaded one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The same issue arises with respect to Exhibit P01661. We have found an error in the English translation; specifically, the frequency in that intercept is recorded incorrectly as 254.950 when it should provide 245.950, and the revised translation has been uploaded under doc ID 0080-4430-A-ET. And if the Defence doesn't object, we'll request again that the Court Officer replace it with the existing translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Court Officer is hereby instructed to replace the English translation of P01661 by the newly uploaded one as mentioned by Ms. Hasan a second ago. Ms. Hasan, have the translations been entirely revised or was it just that you just asked for a revision of those points?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No. Well, we sent them for revision noting that we have seen that this particular issue arises, so I presume CLSS looks at the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Entire document. That's -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what has been done?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart advises that it was only those particular matters I raised that were revised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking this because it now and then happens that there's not only one mistake but there are more. Therefore, the Defence is urged to look at the whole of the document, and at least the error we discovered has been corrected now, but if there's anything more, of course, the Defence could address the matter again. Usually we do that within 48 hours, Mr. Ivetic. And I'm addressing you because the documents were related to the testimony of the present witness. Then we move in -- there was one more, I do understand, in private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Hasan, I did not consult the Rules directly so I have to verify that as well, whether I made any mistakes, because we always learned our students: Don't say a word without having looked at the rules, and I violated that general basic rule but I've seen them in the past. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jevdjevic. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. I also would like to inform you that you'll be invited during one of the breaks to do the same markings on that map as you did yesterday because since a red pencil was used, scanning in order to have a electronic copy was not very successful, so under the supervision of the Registrar and the parties you will be invited to make the same markings but now in black so that it can be scanned again. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, good morning, sir. Now, in relation to the geographic positioning of the two ABiH listening posts, which yesterday we agreed we'd refer to only as the northern and the southern locations without mentioning their names, what comment, if any, do you have as to their possibility of intercepting radio relay routes of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very broad topic. Essentially both locations are very remote from radio relay hubs and points where the radio relay devices of the Drina Corps were located. It's one factor that restricts ability to intercept radio relay communications. Another factor is that these locations were in sites where they cannot find themselves directly inside beams of the electromagnetic waves. They are to the side or in other words on the flanks. And, third in the azimuths of their receiver antennas at intercepting stations were turned in the right direction, then there is a possibility for that to happen. However, during proofing for this testimony and my earlier appearances, I had the occasion to see many intercepts from the two locations we are discussing now. And I noticed that in their reports, at the beginning of every report, the azimuth of the receiver antenna is indicated. And I wish to stress I always remarked that their receiver antenna was turned to face towns and places where our commands were located, not in the direction of our radio relay communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the operation of radio relay devices by the Drina Corps, what was the standard practice as to the power level that they would be operated under?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter used the term "voltage" or "feed." I suppose you don't mean the power supply, but I suppose that you actually mean the power of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could use the B/C/S term, I believe I'm talking about "snaga."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be clear but I'm seeking the common understanding of the parties that the voltage under which you'd operate something doesn't say anything about the power you use in the application of that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Definitely, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, 220 volts would help both for your hairdryer and other machines, which doesn't say anything about the -- I would say the watts, the power used in operating the device which is fed with a 220 volt, if it is 220 volt, not necessarily perhaps, but do the parties agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then that's -- unless the witness would say that I missed the point, we'll just go on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, sir, perhaps I can phrase the question this way: What was the standard practice in the Drina Corps as to what operating power levels the units functioned according to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire standard procedure and the rules that operators had to adhere to before the war and during the war was that if radio relay devices were operating at a shorter distance, they would use less power. Specifically, the radio relay devices we discussed yesterday have the possibility of operating at full power and at lower power. There is a switch that you can turn to full power and decreased power. So at shorter distance, we used less power.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what would be the result in terms of the transmission of the electromagnetic signal from that radio relay device operating at decreased power?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice that would mean that the reach, the range of these electric magnetic waves would be smaller because you're using reduced power, and that is a compulsory measure for protecting information, for protecting the radio relay route from interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you in relation to your last answer to clarify for us: Did you quantify how much smaller the range of the waves would be when operating on the reduced power setting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full power of the radio relay devices we discussed yesterday RRU-800 and FM-200 is 10 watts and reduced power is 5 watts. If the distance between radio relay stations is smaller, then we always operated at reduced power, i.e., 5 watts, to prevent that the electric magnetic waves would reach larger distances and to prevent interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to turn to the Krivaja 95 operation. And first of all, sir, what was your specific tasking in relation to that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that operation, I was an officer whose job it was to implement the plan of communications for the execution of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What role -- what role did the Main Staff play in the establishment of the plan of communications for the operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff had no role. The operation was executed by the Drina Corps, and the plan of communications for that operation was made by the chief of communications of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any encryption devices in use during the Krivaja 95 operation? And now I'm going to first focus on radio devices.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What type of encryption devices were used during that operation for radio devices?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For radio device that operated in the radio network towards subordinated units, we had an encryption device for the scrambling of speech which is called KZU-63.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us how this unit, the KZU-63, would be attached to a radio device to enable encryption?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a small portable device. Using a special cable, you connect it to a radio device, and it's adjusted so that by inserting a particular key or a code into it, the device encrypts speech and sends it, transmits it on the air as encrypted speech. All the other devices that have the same encryption device attached to it with the same key, the same code, are able and only they are able to hear and understand that message.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for a participant of an encrypted radio conversation to inadvertently switch off the KZU-63 device and still participate in the communications with other participants still using encryption, either to send or to receive communication from them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could a participant in the encrypted radio network switch off the KZU-63 encryption device and have it not be noticed by the other participants in the communication?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he turned off his device, he would have practically plugged out of that radio network and he would no longer be able to hear anyone else or be heard by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would there be anything else that would alert the other participants to the radio network that something has happened to that participant whose device has switched off?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the mere fact that they would call him on that network and nobody would answer. They would know that there is a problem with the device because they would not hear him. That was the first indicator for us. So if he's not answering, that means he's not hearing us and we're not hearing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the event that something like that happened, where a participant dropped out of an encrypted radio conversation, what would be the standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The standard procedure would be wherever that participant was, for the encryption man to go there, taking a device which is called key charger, and enable that participant to participate in the encrypted radio network again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any such occurrence during the Krivaja 95 operation where that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that such a thing happened. But if it had happened, that would have been our routine procedure and it's a problem very easily dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- earlier you asked about the planning of this operation and the communications plan which was drafted for that purpose, and the witness told us that it was for the Drina Corps it was drafted. Now, yesterday we looked at -- at two plans, one of 1993, one of 1994. We also looked at the reconstruction of the communications as made by the ABiH after the war. Do we have -- is that plan for the Drina Corps, is that in evidence at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's about to be. It's one of the items I'd on my list, Your Honours. I believe it's 06261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll -- Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene but, Your Honour, you raised the issue of the two plans from yesterday and the dates of them, you mentioned the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The kremen plan is from January 1994. The Drina plan is part of a VRS, VJ, SRK operation known as Drina, which is dated November/December 1993, and the Drina communication network we saw yesterday is part of that operation but at the subordinate level of the Drina Corps. And that's dated January 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, the gist of my request was whether we have -- what we saw yesterday was not summer 1995 but was plans, that's at least how it was explained, plans for communication at earlier periods. And we saw one reconstruction which deals with the summer of 1995 but which was, first of all, a reconstruction, and second was made only after the war. That's how it was introduced. My question is do we have that plan the witness just talked about for Krivaja -- it was -- planned in 1995 for Krivaja within the Drina Corps? That's -- do we have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe we have what the witness is talking about. I'm not sure it is exactly what you'd expect it to be. I can ask the witness to discuss that if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's just for me to be able to follow and not to -- you'll understand that my recollection is not always good enough to know exactly whether a document is among the approximately 10.000 documents which are now in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps then if I actually skip ahead, I can call that up. The number 06261.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, when this comes up, if you could please take a look at and identify the same for us.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the communications plan that was elaborated by the chief of communications of the Drina Corps for the Krivaja 95 operation. According to that plan and in terms of equipment for speech protection that I spoke of a moment ago, well, all of that has to do with this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now looking at this plan, there are some reserve participants listed, two -- two of them. First of all, were those actually used during the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is also a -- there's also an entry for the MUP just above the reserve participants. What position did the MUP or other civilian police have in the communications system for the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this plan, one of the participants in this encrypted radio network was the MUP as well. However, in reality in the field while this operation was being carried out, they never appeared and never participated in this operation and did not have a proper device. So they were not part of the network that I headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would you explain for us there are a -- there are several frequencies, I believe 22 in total that are listed in this document. Can you explain for us how and when these frequencies would be used, paying particular focus to how one would change between frequencies?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we are talking about radio devices. The communications that we carried out according to this plan were carried out with RU-2/2K. And their frequency range is from 30 to 60 megahertz. In case we operated on a particular frequency and if there was some jamming or something like that, we had the following possibility: The person who was handling the network would use a certain table of signals issuing an order to move to one of the reserve frequencies. So in this work-plan, the envisaged frequency number one is the one we see here, and the planner of this activity planned for 21 reserve frequencies as well. Where it says remark here, the way in which a reserve frequency would be used has been explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear, you've identified the radio device in question as a RU-2/2K. First of all, is that the correct denomination?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the correct denomination of that device. Otherwise, that is a device that is fully compatible with the RUP-12. However -- yes, and they also work in the same frequency. They're absolutely the same. However, this is a more modern version, if you will, because a protection device could be plugged into this, so a modified RUP-12 was called RU-2/2K.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the RUP-12 and the RU-2/2K variant of the same, could you identify for us if those were simplex or duplex modes of radio communication?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These radio devices work in simplex only; that is to say, using one frequency. For as long as anyone is speaking on this network, everybody else has to listen because in that case he takes over. It is only when he let's go of the button he used to turn on, then it is only then that the other participants in the conversation can say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I want to move --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, I want to tender the document as the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so, Witness, I do understand that this is something entirely different from what we looked at yesterday? Yesterday we were looking at the radio relay structures, whereas this is just radio communication. Then before we admit the document, I see that there's transcription -- I wouldn't call it a translation error. In the second row of the frequencies, it starts with 12, 13, then again 13, where in the original it reads "14." Now, we could send that back for -- but perhaps it's far more practical to put on the record that it's common understanding between the parties that where it reads 13,272, that it indeed reads 14,272.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's practical and I don't see this becoming an issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't think that this will be the decisive issue. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D910, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. And one of the reasons, if it would be just text it's easy to change it, but this seems to be a very special format which may take far more time to get it right. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to focus on radio relay devices used during the Krivaja 95 operation. Were there any encryption devices in use on radio relay devices during that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe for us what encryption capabilities were used and at which devices.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For carrying out the Krivaja 95 operation, from the forward command post of the Drina Corps in Pribicevac, we established communication with our command of the Drina Corps through RRU-1. Through this device, we had the possibility of sending encoded, encrypted written information, and we also had a KZU-61, and in that way we encoded speech as well. I need to point out that with KZU-61 we could encrypt only speech communication with other participants who had the same device.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for which of the radio relay routes of the Drina Corps that we discussed yesterday did that encryption apply; that is to say, who else -- who were the other participants that had the same capability?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for radio relay routes, the ones we discussed yesterday, we had encrypted communication from the corps command in Vlasenica and the Main Staff. The device for the Main Staff was at Veliki Zep; that is to say, along that line we had this device for encrypting speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you have occasion to come into contact with any UNPROFOR members during the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of the stages of the implementation of this operation when our forces from the direction of Zeleni Jadar were advancing towards Srebrenica, at that moment, according to our information, there was an incident between the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Srebrenica and UNPROFOR. There was an exchange of gun-fire. And on that occasion a member of UNPROFOR was killed. He was located at a check-point in the broader area of Zeleni Jadar. Through communications equipment at the forward command post we received information to the effect that the members of UNPROFOR who were at that check-point used four APCs to move to our side because of this unpleasant situation that they found themselves in. Literally, they withdrew towards our side, towards Zeleni Jadar, and then General Krstic personally - from the forward command post, he was the one who commanded that operation - he sent me to Zeleni Jadar as an active-duty officer so that I take in these UNPROFOR members and bring them to a secure position. I did that. I went in the direction of Zeleni Jadar, and I encountered these four APCs as they were moving towards the broader area of Pribicevac. I turned my vehicle around and brought them to the broader area of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I still have a question which I seek clarification of. You talked about KZU-61. That is different from KZU-63. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood that well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "I need to point out that KZU-61, we could encrypt only speech communication with other participants who had the same device." In what respect is that different from the KZU-63? Because I do understand that for encryption you always use at both ends of the communication devices which are able to, on the one hand side, to encrypt, and on the other side to decrypt. In what respect is the KZU-61 then different from the KZU-63, or is it the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] KZU-63 are devices that are plugged into radio transmitters that soldiers carry on their backs. The dimensions are those of a regular back-pack, and these are portable devices, portable radio devices. As for KZU-61, that is a fixed piece of equipment that we would plug into an RRU-1, and it encoded speech that goes through radio relay equipment between Pribicevac and Veliki Zep on that radio relay route. In order to have this kind of encoded communication with a participant on the other side, that other party needed to have that kind of device too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. You also said that this allowed you for encrypted communication. In relation to the KZU-63, you were asked whether you could switch that off. You said no, it couldn't. Is that the same for KZU-61 or is that different? Because you said: "We had the possibility of sending encoded, encrypted written information, and we also had a KZU-61, and in that way we encoded speech as well." Could you also not switch that off, the KZU-61?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] KZU-61 is a device that technically can be switched off and one can speak openly through an RRU-1. That is the way it was conceived. You can have an open conversation as well. However, when the encoder is turned on, then this speech goes through there protective encoder and then it is encrypted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could return to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. I guess we'll have our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break. Can you tell us how much time you would still need after the break, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes. Mr. Jevdjevic, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the parties and Mr. Registrar will use the break for the new markings. Mr. McCloskey, you were on your feet, but not anymore. We'll take a break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly turn into private session but the witness can be escorted in the courtroom already, although I will deal with one matter before he enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we continue, Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber just gave a ruling that to the extent protective measures for this witness which were granted in the Krstic case would still continue to exist after a decision on the 12th of November, 2008, by the Popovic Chamber that, to the extent that may have been the case, that they're hereby rescinded by retroactive effect, which means that the parties can refer to the evidence given by this witness in the Krstic case not only in terms of substance but also in terms of this testimony be given in the Krstic case. Finally, it is the prerogative of the Presiding Judge of a Chamber to seize any mobile phones that are ringing. I gave authority to my colleagues to seize my mobile phone if mine rings. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we could just finish up with the UNPROFOR members that you encountered, could you please tell us if you recall what date it was that you had that encounter with the UNPROFOR members withdrawing towards VRS lines.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the day when one of them got killed. And I think it could have been the 10th of July, in the middle of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And under what conditions were these UNPROFOR members kept once at the VRS side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following me, they arrived in the broader area of the forward command post Pribicevac. They parked their vehicles in a field, and nobody kept them anywhere. Nobody restricted or controlled them. They were all treated as soldiers who had found themselves in trouble an hour earlier, and they were not kept or mistreated in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to focus on the forward command post for communications at Pribicevac for Krivaja 95. How long did you stay there before completing your duties at that location for that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained until 11 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where did you go then upon completing your duties at the Pribicevac communications command -- forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An hour or two hours before night-fall on the 11th July, I think it could have been 7.00 p.m., I packed up the communications centre at the forward command post. And with all my troops, I set out after what we call elements of the combat disposition who were far in advance of us ahead of the command post, so I passed Srebrenica and Potocari, arriving at the command of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you report to anyone at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command of the Bratunac Brigade, I found my own signalsman, who was carrying the portable radio device for encryption, and he was together with General Krstic in a vehicle. I asked him where General Krstic was, and he answered that Krstic had also come to the Bratunac Brigade Command, so I located General Krstic and then a meeting followed at the command shortly after.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who were the participants in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic; the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic; then the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, General Krstic; the commander of the Zvornik Brigade - I think he was a lieutenant-colonel then - Pandurevic; and to the best of my recollection, all the brigade commanders of the Drina Corps who took part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was the timing of that meeting? What day and what hour are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held on 11 July at the Command of the Bratunac Brigade, and if I remember well, it was from 2200 to 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What topics were the subject matter discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brief analysis of the combat actions of that day was presented at the meeting headed by General Mladic. And after that analysis, he briefed us about the main concept; namely, that on the following day, the 12th July, all the units that participated in Krivaja 95 should regroup and set out to execute the next operation, Stupcanica 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Stupcanica 95, what region or geographic area did that operation involve?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The broader area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was anything else of significance discussed at that meeting that you recall or that you had your attention drawn to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, after General Mladic presented the main concept, that on 12 July all the units should regroup towards Zepa, Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, commander of the Zvornik Brigade, asked to speak, and he presented his opinion that the situation in part of the front line facing Srebrenica was still unclear; meaning, the bulk of the forces of the 28th Division which, according to our intelligence, intended to try to break through, to break out of Srebrenica, and a smaller part of their forces wanted to go towards Zepa. Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic suggested that his forces should wait a little for the situation in Srebrenica to become clearer concerning these forces of the 28th Division who intended to move towards Zepa. And regardless of this thinking of Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, I remember very well that General Mladic said no, no, no, tomorrow everybody goes to Zepa. And he pointed at me and said, "And you, boy, you set up tonight already a forward command post at Krivace between Srebrenica and Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you immediately go to establish a forward command post at Krivace between Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shortly after the official meeting ended and bearing in mind the orders of General Mladic, I stood up immediately and was among the first to leave that room. I gathered my soldiers and picked up my communications centre, which was on a big vehicle, and immediately headed to Vlasenica where the command of the Drina Corps was. Vlasenica itself is further down the road from Srebrenica to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then what else did you do that evening?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got to the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, it was past midnight, and I was reasoning that I wasn't familiar with the location of Krivace where General Mladic had ordered me to set up the communications centre, and it was not easy to do it so late. So I went to the operations centre and used my own common sense because I, as a signalsman, need much less time to get to that location than the brigades who had involved -- who had been involved in the operation around Srebrenica, needed time to assemble and get to Zepa. So either I asked for somebody's permission or decided myself to spend the night in Vlasenica and then replenish my unit with batteries and other things, and then proceed to execute the order on the 12 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And after establishing the communications centre at the -- at the forward command post at Krivace, did at any point in time some new information come to light which changed the situation of the forces available for that operation in relation to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did all the forces that were envisioned for the Zepa operation stay in that region and complete the mission as to the Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation in Zepa began on 14 July in the morning hours. And I remember from the plan of that operation after one day of fighting, one part of the Zvornik Brigade was pulled out, and this part was commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic himself, and was ordered to go back to the area of that brigade because of the problems that their units had in fighting the 28th Division that was trying to break out of encirclement and link up with their own forces, the forces of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your knowledge and understanding of the threat posed by the problems that the Zvornik units had in fighting with the 28th Division that was trying to break out of encirclement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Major Dragan Obrenovic, Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, called me on the phone personally, since we have been good friends from childhood and we finished all the military schools together. He sounded panicked. He was calling me at my forward command post knowing that I was close to General Krstic, and he asked me to try to convince General Krstic, to get through to him the urgency of the situation he was facing in fighting the 28th Division, because the Zvornik Brigade had deployed all its available forces to hold the front line facing Tuzla and its elite unit and its reserve unit that it had was already on the front line towards Zepa, so he had literally taken out one platoon to confront the whole division. He said that he had already contacted many other people but they had shown little understanding for the seriousness of his position, so he asked me to reason and convince General Krstic that it was absolutely necessary to bring back Vinko Pandurevic and his units to help him in his fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in terms of where this fighting was going on, did you have an appreciation from the information that you received of where precisely this fighting was going on between the 28th Division and the platoon that had been mustered up by Major Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my estimate and my knowledge about that battle, the fighting was taking place along the transversal where even earlier the sabotage groups had contact with the units in Tuzla. It's across Pobudje, the broader area of Konjevic Polje, Cerska, Udrc, towards Tuzla. So somewhere in the area of Crni Vrh in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions both on behalf of myself, General Mladic, and the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Jevdjevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You find Ms. Hasan to your right. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just to start, can you tell us what -- what -- what's your nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jevdjo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And was that what people would call you during the war time as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how they addressed me, those who were in closer communication with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Are there any other Jevdjos that you know of in the Drina Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Drina Corps, no. In the protection corps -- regiment there was my brother. Everybody called him Jevdjo too. And there was this other man in the Visegrad Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's go to your testimony in relation to Zeleni Jadar. Now, you testified yesterday, do I understand you correctly, that you were only involved in the operation to the extent of setting up the communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you made a brief reference to a document that suggested that you had been in a leadership role; do you recall, recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation I received was "leadership"? In our country, only the commander and the Chief of Staff can be leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to 65 ter 19555, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps this document will help refresh your recollection on what role you had. So what this is, it's an order from the Drina Corps Command. It's dated the 29th of May, 1995. We see that it's marked urgent. And it relates to the order for the taking over of Zeleni Jadar, of the Zeleni Jadar sector. And among others, it's addressed to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, and the Skelani separate battalion. It provides at the beginning: "Following UNPROFOR departure from the Zeleni Jadar check-point, Muslim forces will probably try to place Zeleni Jadar under their control." "In order to prevent the incursion of enemy forces into Zeleni Jadar and place the Zeleni Jadar factory complex and the Skelani-Podravanje road under our control, I hereby order the following ..." And this is an order from General Zivanovic. If we look at item 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we look at item 3, it provides, the order, again, of General Zivanovic: "Engage the following officers from the Drina Corps command to command the attacking forces in the Zeleni Jadar sector." And we see three names: Colonel Obrad Vicic, Colonel Stojan Veletic, and Major Milenko Jevdjevic. And these are persons you made reference to yesterday during your testimony. So according to this order from General Zivanovic, you were supposed to be a leader of this attack. In fact, this was an order that you were to lead this attack. Does that help you remember about what role you had?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just go on reading, that is to say read the next sentence, just where you stopped, you will see that it says here: "I will personally command the forces from the forward command post of the Drina Corps at Pribicevac." Major-General Zivanovic says that this attribute of command and control only belongs to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So you're denying what it says very clearly in this order, that he was engaging you to command the attacking forces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably this is a misinterpretation or a mistranslation. It says here that Zivanovic is telling himself that he will personally command the forces from the forward command post. Everybody else assists him in particular areas. I was the man in charge of the field of communications, and that is unequivocal and I never denied that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the order is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer 65 ter 19555 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's comment, Ms. Hasan, that the order is clear. But I do understand you tender it. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7130 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday in relation to this -- in relation to this attack that it was carried out without a single bullet being fired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, it always assists us if you would have a page reference. If not, then of course it's no drama, but...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I actually don't have one for this one but I certainly can look it up and bring it to your attention as soon as I find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll find it anyhow. But if you have it there, then I can immediately follow what you're referring to. That's the issue. But I'll search for "bullet" and then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we have P01153, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, it is 31878. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, this is an order from General Zivanovic. It's dated the 2nd of June, 1995, regarding the restoration of the control over the facilities and the Zeleni Jadar asphalt road. And we see it's issued to the command of the Bratunac Brigade and the commander of the Drina Corps Manoeuvre Battalion. And it states that the conditions were right to "launch the final stage of liberating Zeleni Jadar in its entirety." Are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During proofing, I did have an opportunity to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, to sum it up, it outlines the steps of how to remove a UN observation post at Zeleni Jadar, and if we look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: On page 1 at the end, and this is at the end of the page in the B/C/S, and the third bullet point, I believe, from the top of the English. It's on the second page of the English, I apologise. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And there it says -- in outlining how to take over this OP, it says: "If they fail," and this is a reference to UNPROFOR, "to follow the order," of surrender, which is previously discussed, "one should fire a Zolja hand-held rocket-launcher into a power generator, with readiness to neutralise a personnel carrier, while taking care to avoid physically injuring any UNPROFOR personnel." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, if we look down in the English on page 2, and it's about the fourth bullet point in the English, and I think we have to turn now to page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It provides: "If the UNPROFOR continue threatening to use weapons towards Legenda, use a Zolja to neutralise a personnel carrier." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you'd agree that the Legenda referenced here is Milan Jolovic from the Drina Wolves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That unit was called the Podrinje Detachment of special forces battalion of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And as far as you remember, did that unit also take part in this attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now if we scroll down in the B/C/S, and in the English we have to turn the page to the signature page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, it was put to you that the name was the Drina Wolves. Is that confirmed by you as well, that that was the name used to refer to that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Its official name in our establishment was not the Drina Wolves but they themselves called themselves that, so others called them that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now if we look at the handwritten note there at the bottom, it reads: "For Skelani SPB (Jevdo should convey) self-propelled guns to be included at 0500." That would be you, a message that you were to convey; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, this order to remove UNPROFOR from their observation point, which details calls to surrender and then to -- to use weapons to disengage them, that was carried out, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, this telegram was received at the command of the Bratunac Brigade, and someone from the command of the Bratunac Brigade probably in his own hand for some reason stated, probably thinking of the communications plan, that Jevdjo would convey or transmit the plan of communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm stopping you there. Could you please answer the question. The question was whether the order, and the details were given by Ms. Hasan, was carried out or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hasan said -- well, this speaks only about the plan if members of UNPROFOR do this, if they do that, so these are assumptions. This entire order is based on assumptions. Or, rather, on a sequence of steps. If somebody does this, then this should be applied. So this is not an order for attack for combat activities because otherwise what would have been written in the letterhead would have been order to attack. It is only an order for the territory held by the Drina Corps that positions should be moved from one line to another; that is to say, within that framework that is under its control, of course, everything outside the protected area and outside the Muslim positions. So this was just relocation, and that is also what the title says, relocating one's own lines to a better territory so that our territory would be in our rear, behind us. And also include self-propelled weapons. That is not what I am supposed to convey. With the best of intentions and to interpret this as a soldier who took part in this, maybe this means that the Bratunac Brigade has, just in case, artillery prepared somewhere, include self-propelled guns. That is not what is stated here that I should convey that. These are two different statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, did you intend to take the witness back again to the stamp or did you just wanted an answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, absolutely, I just wanted him to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, apparently it's of some concern to you what is written at the bottom here, but that is not what you were asked about. I think you explained that in this order various scenarios are described and therefore you say it's not an order. At the same time, if at the end of the order it says Legenda and Petrovic shall take control of the UNPROFOR check-point and make detailed arrangement before continuing along the asphalt road crossing Jadar, I mean, that's clearly an order, isn't it, although some possible scenarios, what would have happened in between, are described. But if you say it's not an order, this last paragraph certainly at least very much resembles what an order is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire document, the entire operation, was not conceived as an order to attack. Only to relocate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one talked about an order to attack. It was just referred to whether this order was put in place, yes or no. You told us already that some of the portions were written in a way as if this happens, then do that; if this happens, then do that. That's clear. Ms. Hasan will now put further questions to you, and I would urge you to carefully listen to what she wants to know rather than what you consider relevant to tell her. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, and please try to just answer the question, was this order of General Zivanovic carried out? Simple: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, that's not an appropriate question. The witness has rightly explained that the order contains various possibilities. Now, if you want to know whether it was carried out, you can, as I did, either refer to the last part, where there's no such conditions, or you should put to the witness did they point weapons, was this said or not, because all the same -- you have to be specific there. You can't ask a yes or no on the basis of this order. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, it -- would you agree with me that -- and you having reviewed this -- this document, that it was essentially, leaving aside whether you claim it happened or not, an order to terrorise or scare UNPROFOR and get them in -- to leave the OP. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 32038.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, this is the -- what's going to appear is your testimony from the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we could e-court page 54.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you're asked at line 17, and I'll read this out slowly so you can follow along: "Q. And I understand how important that was. And, basically, this is an order to scare the daylights out of UNPROFOR and get them to leave that OP; correct? " And your answer was: "Well, more or less, yes." Do you stand by that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that part of my testimony, but this is probably, again, a case of taking things out of context. If UNPROFOR were to put up resistance, that is how the entire order is treated. If UNPROFOR were not to resist with using weapons in any way, the order says very nicely that our forces would just pass through and put their positions within their own area of responsibility. In case they resist, then there is an envisaged scenario; namely, that in a way it be made known to UNPROFOR by firing a gun into the air, et cetera, that quite simply they should not interfere in that part of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And since you have provided us with your interpretation today saying parts of it wasn't followed and parts it was and it was conditional, well, let's look at what you said in Popovic at line 7: "Q. So we can conclude that this order was followed, can't we? "A. Well, the person who issued the order would probably know that best if he were to carry out an analysis. Last week, I spoke in detail about the events I remember from that period of time. "Q. Well, was it carried out or not?" And your answer was: "It was, but later on some people were dissatisfied with this because was it enough to secure those factories, because the Muslim side could control the Zeleni Jadar area with fire-power. But I remember that the Zeleni Jadar-Jasenova road could be used after this, and that was very important for our units on the ground there." So, do you stand by that testimony you gave in the Popovic -- before the Popovic Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. Is this an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break now. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we see Exhibit P02100.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, this is the regular combat report from the 3rd of June, 1995, which we looked at yesterday. And it's in relation to this document that you had testified at transcript page 31878, lines 22 to 25: "That whoever it was who wrote this probably wanted to exaggerate his own contribution to these events." Now, you may recall that this document set out that the population, the civilians in that area, left in panic. So according to you, sir, that would have been something impressive to tell your superiors, or to tell a superior?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that somebody tried to exaggerate, I meant the entire document. Quite simply, one of the hundreds of sentences in this document; namely, that the population had fled in panic. And my testimony was that there was no population living there, and therefore they could not have fled there panic. So this flight of civilians would not be impressive for any officer. But my testimony was there was nobody living there in the first place, and therefore they could not flee in panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look at page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S -- oh, sorry, I apologise. The English - keep it - it starts on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And it says: "In a very precise and professional operation, they forced the strong and courageous UNPROFOR check-point in Zeleni Jadar to withdraw in panic to Srebrenica." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It looks like it's also page 2 in the -- sorry, page 1 in the B/C/S, item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just at the beginning there. I'll give you an opportunity to read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps it can be enlarged a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And if we turn to item 3. That's the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It says: "We have -- we have had no casualties. We expended small amounts of ammunition and three Zoljas, hand-held rockets." Now, that's consistent with General Zivanovic's order of the 2nd of June, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean it's consist with the order? What is it that you are specifically citing and then saying that it is in keeping with General Zivanovic's order?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, for one thing, that ammunition, including Zoljas, were used.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you and I said in all my previous testimonies that to the best of my knowledge this action was carried out without a single bullet fired. It was completed by 9.00 in the morning. We transferred our forces from one area to another, and not a single bullet was fired let alone three Zoljas. My knowledge from that period does not tally with what this report says.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what DutchBat officer Major Franken says.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And that's P1417. Your Honours, that's his admitted statement in this case. If we could see page 10 in the English and page 17 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And he describes the VRS attack on OP Echo in paragraph 38, and he says: "On 3 June 1995 the VRS attacked OP Echo. We got report through Bravo Company, the company responsible for that area, that there was some movement in front of OP Echo. The movement proved to be Serb infantry. Then the Serb infantry used the loud-speaker to tell the OP that they had to go, they had to withdraw because the Serbs wanted to come in. B Company asked me permission to do that which I denied. Then they came under attack and in the end the Serbs took OP Echo over and the crew withdrew in the very last moment with my authorisation. The attack was conducted by about 40 infantry supported by a tank, (T55), a main battle tank, and a gun on the edge, ridge at Zeleni Jadar. The observation tower was hit by the firing main battle tank and the area was fired at by the anti-aircraft gun standing up there used to support the Serb attack." So, Mr. Jevdjevic, do still maintain that no force was used in this attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge because we were listening with our own ears to hear what would happen, and we were expecting gun-fire at any moment. But then in the early morning hours, we received reports that our forces had just crossed over to the line they wished to reach. So that event remained in my memory as the only planned combat activity where we accomplished the mission without combat, and I stand by the evidence I gave yesterday and earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, then, that the report that is -- that bears your name that we just previously looked at, that -- that would have meant that you were operating outside of your regular communications duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So you could have authored that report, despite the fact that you were -- you claim you were just -- just engaged in communications?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter just told me that you claim I could have authored that report. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What I'm asking is, that report bears your name. Now you claim that that is -- that couldn't have been you, okay? But it would mean, right, the fact that it bears your name, that you were acting outside your regular communications duties.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I am getting a very strange interpretation or I failed to understand your logic. I maintained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll phrase the question again. If you would have been the author of that document, which you say you're not, would that mean that such activity, writing such a report and being involved it as described, that that would have been beyond, outside what your real functions were; that is, being engaged in communications. Would you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, I take it that this resolves the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you told us - I'm going to move on to a different topic - that you were at the Pribicevac forward command post during the Krivaja 95 operation. Could you tell us when it was that General Mladic arrived at the IKM on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And is that 10.00 in the morning or 10.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do you recall how long he stayed on the 10th of July at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very location of the forward command post, he spent very little time. He was going further on towards the forward lines where the observation posts were, and it was not within my field of vision. But he stayed in the broader area of the forward command post perhaps until later afternoon. He was at the observation posts near the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How far were these observation posts from the command post -- forward command post?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no communications, as you -- turn, please. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, if someone was trying to reach General Mladic from the Main Staff or from Vlasenica, they could reach him, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And General Mladic was also at the Pribicevac forward command post on the 11th of July; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And could you share with us when he arrived and when he left.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he arrived before noon; and he left the forward command post in the early afternoon, around 3.00, 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And as you were at the forward command post, do you agree that the chain of command remained intact throughout that Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object to the question as being unclear. Which chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you perhaps be a bit more precise. I think I understand your question but to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the VRS chain of command and the command over this Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I would ask that she split up the two questions. Those are two different chains of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then the witness can answer the question. And if there's any need to follow up, then we'll find that from his answer. Witness, could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operation was commanded by the Drina Corps, and that chain of command remained unchanged throughout the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness also, was there anything -- you said within the Drina Corps the chain of command functioned normally. Of course, the Drina Corps was under the command of the Main Staff of the VRS, the main command. Was there anything there which you think was interrupted in any way, chain of command from the Drina Corps up and down from the Main Staff and command to the extent you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything functioned normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both at the level of the Drina Corps and at the level above the Drina Corps, as far as you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't understand what you're asking me. Everything functioned normally. The Drina Corps was carrying out the operation. It established the forward command post. The forward command post was commanded by someone from the Drina Corps. In this case, General Krstic. In Vlasenica, where the command of the Drina Corps is based, it continued to function according to the previous plan. And the Main Staff and their command, in their location, continued to function according to their plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, I'm going to move on to the evidence you just gave towards the end of your testimony today about this meeting that you claim took place on the night of 11 July. And this is, in fact, an account that you have been given -- that you gave in the Krstic case, and this is when General Krstic tried as well to put that meeting on the 11th of July. You were aware of that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you claiming should have been clear to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, that General Krstic was also claiming that the meeting you were referring to took place on the 11th July and not the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what General Krstic claimed, but I know that the meeting that I, too, attended was held on 11 July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, we happen to have the contemporaneous diary that was taken by Mirko Trivic who is the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we could take a look at those; it's Exhibit P01467. And if we could turn to page 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you see there, it says: "Order: Remain at the line reached. The brigade commanders are to come to the Drina Corps IKM in Bratunac by 2100 hours via Srebrenica and Potocari (the Bratunac Brigade KM)," command. Now, in fact, you attended the meeting that took place at 2100 hours with all the brigade commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that I said that, to the best of my recollection, that meeting began around 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you did travel through -- from -- from the forward command post at Pribicevac through Srebrenica and Potocari; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Mirko Trivic goes on to record that General Mladic arrived at 2200 hours. That also accords with when you've told us this meeting took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although this thing that resembles a diary is something I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, he then notes after congratulations and greetings, and in brackets: [As read] "(Despite the fact that Vinko Pandurevic and I warned him [sic] that the soldiers should rest) he ordered ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The English reads: "I told him," not "I warned him."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, does that -- is that consistent with your recollection of what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what about the next point he notes down: "By 0800 hours tomorrow, General Krstic must prepare a decision for the liberation of Zepa!" Does that accord with your recollection of what took place at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fact is in keeping with what I already testified to; namely, that General Mladic ordered that everyone should move the next day to the operation in Zepa. Now whether he ordered Krstic to prepare a decision or not, I don't remember such details, but I remember our destination was Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that General Mladic addressed the soldiers who were to take part in the Zepa operation in Vijogor village before they left? You were aware of that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, if we turn back to page 25 in the English and the B/C/S. And we can go through this page by page to where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But you will see here that Mirko Trivic recorded this meeting as having taken place on the 12th of July, not on the 11th July as you claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you are saying "this meeting." I read here 0900 hours. I don't know if that -- I think it refers to 9.00 a.m., but we are talking about a meeting late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct. So it will help, then, to just turn to the next page so there's -- we have 0900 hours, 12 July 1995. His notes continue. And we can go to the following page. And we can continue to the next page. We come to the page we were just looking at. And when we turn to the page after that, the notes continue. And he reports on events at 2300 hours. And if we follow along to the next page, we see the next diary entry, Wednesday, 13 July, 1000 hours. And, Your Honours, I can find the reference to the testimony on this diary, if that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge raised the issue, so I leave it in his hands to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we went through several pages and we saw an entry, 11th July, 12th July, and then here a reference to a 13th July. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I suppose, then, you are claiming that Trivic's diary is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only maintain that I'm absolutely certain the meeting was held at around 2200 hours on 11 July. There are some events that I remember less well, some others I remember better, but I maintain with absolute certainty that that meeting was held around 2200 hours on 11 July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So this document is wrong, this diary is wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't go into what Colonel Trivic wrote or whether he was mistaken about the date. But out of all the events from that period, my clearest memory, an unmistakable memory is that that meeting was held on 11 July and began around 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now before you left this meeting, did anyone, including General Krstic, give you any precise orders about the communications that were to be set up for this Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, how was it that you knew which units precisely were to be involved in that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because General Mladic ordered that evening that all the units that had taken part in the operation in Srebrenica, all be transferred to the operation in Zepa. That's how I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did you ever receive orders on the set-up of the communications for this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic ordered me. That was perfectly enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So you did not receive any other orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit D00290, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in the -- in the meantime, sir, were you aware you were -- I take it, then, that you were not aware that Krstic issued Zepa attack order on the 13th of July and that in that attack order he provides orders for the set-up of communications at the Drina Corps forward command post. And this is the order appears on our screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 4 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We see here that on the 13th of July at -- under item 10: "Command and communications." And the Chief of Staff orders: "The Drina Corps forward command post in Krivace shall start working at 1800 hours on 13 July 1995. "Communications shall be ready for the attack at 0600 hours on 14 July 1995." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Krivace, that's where the forward command post for the operation was established; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you're claiming that you did not act pursuant to these orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was written two days after the decision was made and the basic concept of the commander was generated for the operation in Zepa. All these decisions have to be formalised in writing, and thus in every order there is a paragraph that determines where the forward command post would be, when it would start operating, what the communications system would be like. It all has to be written in the order because the army is such an institution. All the points in the order have to be specified in a particular sequence. When this order was written, I had been in the forward command post already one day and a half. I was setting up the communications system and I was waiting for the other units to arrive in the area -- in the sector of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
